title: Postnatal physiology and routine assessment
blurb: Carry out the NICE NG194 postnatal check: involution and lochia, perineum, bladder and bowels, and the timing of each postnatal contact.
question: Zainab, 26, gave birth vaginally 7 hours ago with a second-degree tear. She has not passed urine since the birth and her bladder is palpable. She is keen to go home this afternoon. What should the midwife do before transfer to community care?

teach.h: The body returning to its non-pregnant state
teach.body: Formally: the postnatal period follows the birth while the reproductive organs return towards their non-pregnant state (involution) and the woman recovers physically and emotionally. In plain English: the uterus shrinks and stops bleeding, the perineum heals, the bladder and bowels recover, and she adjusts to life with a baby. Routine assessment at every contact checks that each of these is on track and spots deviations early.

items: Record temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate.
Examine the placenta and membranes for completeness; transfer to obstetric-led care if incomplete.
Make an early assessment of her emotional and psychological response to labour and birth.
Check she has voided: if after 6 hours her bladder is palpable and she cannot pass urine, advise catheterisation and consider transfer to obstetric-led care.

steps.label: Bladder function
steps.sub: Measure the volume of the first void

steps.label: Information
steps.sub: What to expect, pelvic floor, who to contact

teach.caption: If the baby has not passed meconium, advise parents to seek advice if this has not happened within 24 hours of birth.

teach.h: Lochia: tell her what to expect
teach.body: Discuss the vaginal bleeding to expect after the birth (lochia) and advise her to seek medical advice if bleeding is sudden or very heavy, increases, she passes clots, placental tissue or membranes, or she has signs of infection such as pain, fever, shivering, or an unpleasant smell. If she seeks advice, assess severity and be aware that anaemia or a booking weight under 50 kg can worsen the consequences of secondary PPH.

items.label: First midwife visit after transfer
items.sub: face to face, usually at home (1.1.14)

root.label: Ask about the perineum
root.sub: pain, need for pain relief, smell, swelling, breakdown

children.label: Offer examination by midwife or doctor
Urgent referral, seen the same day

teach.caption: Good hygiene: shower the perineum daily, change pads frequently, wash hands before and after (1.2.16). Consider a validated pain scale (1.2.17).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Zainab on the postnatal ward
teach.body: Seven hours after the birth Zainab has not voided and her bladder is palpable. More than 6 hours have passed, so the midwife advises catheterisation and considers transfer to obstetric-led care (NG235 1.12.1). Bladder function must be assessed before transfer home by measuring the first void (NG194 1.1.10), so discharge waits. The midwife also checks her perineum, lochia, observations and mood, and observes an effective feed.

teach.text: "Has she passed urine?" is not enough. NICE asks for the VOLUME of the first void to be measured before transfer home, because a small void can hide retention. And the first community midwife visit is within 36 hours of transfer, not 72.

items: After birth: observations, uterine contraction, lochia, placenta, early emotional check, voiding.
Palpable bladder and unable to void after 6 hours: advise catheterisation.
Before transfer: measure first void volume, assess baby, observe at least 1 effective feed.
Each contact: mood, infection, bleeding, bladder, bowels, breasts, VTE, anaemia, pre-eclampsia, perineum or wound.
First midwife visit within 36 hours; health visitor 7-14 days; GP at 6-8 weeks.

summary: You can now carry out a structured postnatal assessment, from the checks straight after birth to each community contact. You know when bladder function, lochia or perineal healing needs action and when each postnatal visit should happen.

A.q: Before Lucy, 24, is transferred home from the birth centre, how should the midwife assess her bladder function?
options: Ask whether she has passed urine yet
Dipstick the first sample for protein
Measure the volume of her first void
Palpate the bladder at transfer
A.why: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer to community care, assess bladder function by measuring the volume of the first void after giving birth.

whyNot.0: Asking whether she has voided does not show whether she emptied her bladder; NICE asks for the volume to be measured.
whyNot.1: Proteinuria testing relates to pre-eclampsia, not to bladder function after birth.
whyNot.3: Palpation alone does not replace measuring the first void volume.

A.q: Within what time should the first postnatal midwife visit take place after a woman is transferred home from hospital?
options: Within 36 hours of transfer
Within 72 hours of transfer
Within 24 hours of the birth
Within 7 days of transfer
A.why: NG194 1.1.14: the first postnatal visit by a midwife should take place within 36 hours after transfer of care from the place of birth or after a home birth, face to face and usually at home.

whyNot.1: 72 hours is the deadline for the newborn physical examination (NIPE), not the first midwife visit.
whyNot.2: The clock starts at transfer of care, not at the birth, and the limit is 36 hours.
whyNot.3: 7 to 14 days is the suggested window for the first health visitor visit (1.1.15).

A.q: Which instruction about lochia should the midwife give Emma, 30, on day 2?
options: Seek advice if the bleeding is bright red at any point
Seek advice if any bleeding continues past day 3
Seek advice if the loss changes from red to brown
Seek advice if she passes clots or the loss increases
A.why: NG194 1.2.13: advise women to seek medical advice if bleeding is sudden or very heavy, increases, they pass clots, placental tissue or membranes, or there are signs of infection.

whyNot.0: Red lochia is expected in the early days; the concern is heavy, increasing or sudden bleeding.
whyNot.1: Lochia normally continues well beyond day 3, so this would cause needless worry.
whyNot.2: A change from red to brown is part of the normal pattern, not a warning sign.

B.q: Nadia, 32, gave birth 6 and a half hours ago. She cannot pass urine and her bladder is palpable. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Encourage oral fluids and reassess in 2 hours
Advise catheterisation and consider transfer to obstetric-led care
Give a laxative and repeat the bladder scan tomorrow
Transfer her home with advice to phone if she has not voided by midnight
B.why: NG235 1.12.1: if after 6 hours her bladder is palpable and she is unable to pass urine, advise catheterisation and consider transferring her (with her baby) to obstetric-led care.

whyNot.0: More fluids with a full bladder she cannot empty delays treatment of retention.
whyNot.2: A laxative does not treat urinary retention, and waiting until tomorrow risks bladder damage.
whyNot.3: Bladder function must be assessed before transfer home (NG194 1.1.10).

B.q: On day 4 at home, Chloe, 28, says her perineal stitches have come apart. What should the community midwife arrange?
options: A GP appointment within the next week
Review at the 6 to 8 week check
Same-day specialist maternity review
Salt baths and review in 2 days
B.why: NG194 1.2.20: if the perineal wound breaks down, refer urgently to specialist maternity services to be seen the same day.

whyNot.0: A routine GP appointment within the week is too slow for wound breakdown.
whyNot.1: Waiting until the 6 to 8 week check misses the same-day standard.
whyNot.3: Self-care and a 2-day review do not meet the same-day referral standard.

B.q: Before transfer home, Baby Ali has not yet passed meconium at 10 hours old. What should the midwife tell his parents?
options: Seek advice if no meconium has passed by 24 hours of age
Seek advice if no meconium has passed by 72 hours of age
Seek advice if no meconium has passed by day 5 blood spot
Seek advice if no wet nappy has appeared by day 3
B.why: NG194 1.1.10 and 1.3.2: if the baby has not passed meconium, advise parents to seek advice if this does not happen within 24 hours; failure may indicate a serious disorder.

whyNot.1: 72 hours is the NIPE examination deadline; meconium is expected within 24 hours.
whyNot.2: Day 5 is when the blood spot is taken, far too late for delayed meconium.
whyNot.3: This changes the question to urine; the specific NICE advice concerns meconium within 24 hours.

C.q: Rebecca, 35, is 9 days after a caesarean birth. At a home visit she reports increasing pain around her scar, and her wound is red with an unpleasant discharge. Which part of the NG194 assessment is this most directly testing?
options: Symptoms of venous thromboembolism
Wound healing and wound infection
Symptoms and signs of pre-eclampsia
Psychological and emotional wellbeing
C.why: NG194 1.2.3: for women who have had a caesarean, the midwife assesses wound healing and symptoms of wound infection. Redness and offensive discharge point to infection, needing referral (1.2.6).

whyNot.0: VTE presents with leg swelling and tenderness, breathlessness or chest pain, not a red discharging wound.
whyNot.2: Pre-eclampsia signs include headache, visual disturbance and raised BP, not wound discharge.
whyNot.3: Mood is assessed at every contact, but these findings are physical signs of wound infection.

C.q: Ruth, 22, had her baby at home 4 hours ago. She has not yet passed urine, the midwife has observed an effective breastfeed, and her observations are normal. Before leaving, which further step does NG194 require?
options: Book the GP check for 2 weeks
Measure the volume of her first void
Arrange a hospital review tomorrow
Weigh the baby before the first feed
C.why: NG194 1.1.10 applies before the midwife leaves after a home birth as well as before hospital transfer: assess bladder function by measuring the volume of the first void.

whyNot.0: The routine GP postnatal check is at 6 to 8 weeks (1.2.7), not 2 weeks.
whyNot.2: A routine hospital review is not needed for a well woman after a home birth.
whyNot.3: Birth weight is measured soon after the first hour (NG235 1.11.14), and the first feed has already happened; it is not the NG194 pre-departure requirement.

C.q: At her day 5 visit, Olivia, 29, says her perineal pain is getting worse and she needs more painkillers. Her booking weight was 48 kg and she is anaemic. Which statement guides the midwife best?
options: Worsening pain is expected by day 5 and needs reassurance
Her low booking weight means bleeding is less likely
Offer a perineal examination and assess for infection
Advise ice packs and review again at the 6 week check
C.why: NG194 1.2.15 and 1.2.18: pain not resolving or worsening and increasing need for pain relief are concerns; offer examination of the perineum by a midwife or doctor. Anaemia and booking weight under 50 kg also worsen the consequences of secondary PPH (1.2.14).

whyNot.0: Worsening pain and rising analgesic use are warning signs, not expected findings.
whyNot.1: A booking weight under 50 kg worsens the consequences of secondary PPH; it does not make bleeding less concerning.
whyNot.3: Waiting until 6 weeks delays assessment of a possible infection or breakdown.

reteach.title: Head to toe, every visit
reteach.question: A simple way to never miss a postnatal check is to work through her body in order. What does that sweep look like?

blocks.h: Mind first, then top to bottom
blocks.body: Start by asking how she is feeling and what worries her, because mood matters at every contact. Then work down: breasts and nipples, the uterus and lochia, the perineum or caesarean wound, bladder and bowels, then legs (VTE). Throughout, look for signs of infection, anaemia and pre-eclampsia. Anything abnormal gets referred.

blocks.text: Two different 6-hour and 36-hour numbers: palpable bladder with no void by 6 HOURS after birth needs catheterisation; the first community midwife visit is within 36 HOURS of transfer.

explain.body: Check for successful voiding after the birth. If after 6 hours her bladder is palpable and she cannot pass urine, advise catheterisation and consider transfer to obstetric-led care. Before transfer home, measure the volume of the first void.

items.label: palpable bladder, no void: advise catheter

test.q: Which finding at 6 hours after birth means the midwife should advise catheterisation?
options: She has voided 400 mL since the birth
Her lochia is heavier when she first stands
She has not yet opened her bowels since birth
Her bladder is palpable and she cannot void
test.why: NG235 1.12.1: palpable bladder and inability to pass urine after 6 hours means advise catheterisation.

whyNot.0: She has voided a measurable amount; the trigger is a palpable bladder with no void.
whyNot.1: Lochia pooling on standing is common; it is not a catheter trigger.
whyNot.2: Bowels opening is not expected within 6 hours and is not a catheter trigger.

explain.body: At each postnatal midwife contact assess psychological wellbeing and physical health: infection, pain, vaginal loss, bladder, bowels, breasts, VTE, anaemia, pre-eclampsia, plus perineal healing after vaginal birth or wound healing after caesarean.

test.q: Which assessment is part of every postnatal midwife contact under NG194, whatever the mode of birth?
options: Measuring fundal height in centimetres
Symptoms and signs of thromboembolism
Routine full blood count
Urinalysis for glucose
test.why: NG194 1.2.3 lists symptoms and signs of thromboembolism among the checks for all women at every postnatal midwife contact.

whyNot.0: Measuring fundal height in centimetres is not an NG194 postnatal check.
whyNot.2: A blood test is not a routine part of every contact; symptoms and signs of anaemia are assessed.
whyNot.3: Routine urinalysis for glucose is not on the NG194 list.

explain.body: Explain what bleeding to expect. Seek advice if bleeding is sudden or very heavy, increases, she passes clots, tissue or membranes, or there are signs of infection or an unpleasant smell. Anaemia and booking weight under 50 kg worsen the consequences of secondary PPH.

test.q: Which lochia description should prompt Amy, 25, to seek medical advice?
options: Loss that is heavier when she first stands up
Loss changing to a paler colour over days
Loss with an unpleasant smell and shivering
Loss that is lighter than her first day
test.why: NG194 1.2.13: offensive-smelling loss with fever or shivering suggests infection and needs medical advice.

whyNot.0: A brief gush on standing is common and is not on the NICE list.
whyNot.1: Gradual paling of lochia is the expected pattern.
whyNot.3: Lighter loss over time is reassuring.

explain.body: At each contact ask about pain that is not resolving or is worsening, increasing need for pain relief, smelly discharge, swelling, or wound breakdown. Offer an examination if there is concern. Wound breakdown: urgent referral, seen the same day.

test.q: Which risk factor makes persistent postnatal perineal pain more likely?
options: Assisted vaginal birth
Birth in water
Physiological third stage
Early skin-to-skin contact
test.why: NG194 1.2.22 lists episiotomy or tear, assisted vaginal birth, wound infection or breakdown, and a birth experienced as traumatic as risk factors for persistent perineal pain.

whyNot.1: Water birth is not listed as a risk factor for persistent perineal pain.
whyNot.2: Third-stage management is not on the NG194 list.
whyNot.3: Skin-to-skin contact is not associated with perineal pain.
